newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's new chancellor Klima lies low.
newsitem.headline: Austria's new chancellor Klima lies low.

text.p: Austria's chancellor-designate Viktor Klima seemed likely to shun the media again on Monday, two days after outgoing chancellor Franz Vranitzky resigned and handed him the reins of power.

Vranitzky, 59, caught Austria off-guard when he announced his resignation after nearly 11 years in office and nominated Klima, his finance minister, as leader of the Social Democratic Party and the new chancellor.
Klima, 49, has yet to appear in public since the announcement, choosing to leave Vranitzky, a close friend and confidant, in the spotlight and newshounds to speculate on his movements.
Social Democrats issued a statement saying Klima would hold a news conference on Monday with Vranitzky but they cancelled the meeting less than an hour later.
Asked why it had been cancelled, a Social Democrat official said: "He (Klima) has engagements tomorrow afternoon."
Klima, riding a wave of popularity after his deft handling of the privatisation of key bank Creditanstalt last week, was apparently reluctant to take over the top job.
Vranitzky said he had to persuade him. "He said he had no intention to take this job, but I convinced him my plans were better in the medium to long term," he said.
While Klima kept out of sight, Vranitzky, a former national basketball star turned banker and politician, gave his valedictory news conference to a packed crowd of reporters.

He said the handover to Klima represented a smooth transition and continuity in Social Democrat policies. "I am convinced Klima is not only capable of building a bridge into the next century, but is also capable of crossing it," he said.

Vranitzky, one of Austria's all-time popular politicians, rated his tenure's greatest achievement as guiding an initially reluctant Alpine republic into the European Union, ending half a century of Cold War isolation.

Outside Austria, he is credited with doing much towards restoring the country's image abroad after the controversial presidency of Kurt Waldheim, who was criticised for trying to hide his past in Hitler's Wehrmacht.

At home, while he won respect for steering his coalition government through often choppy waters, his party's popularity waned over the past decade and lost votes largely to the far right Freedom Party led by Joerg Haider.
Vranitzky conceded that his party had underestimated the politicial rise of Haider's nationalist far right. With hindsight, he said, he would have handled Haider differently.
"Perhaps the Social Democrats were a bit too late and did not do enough to unmask his strategy of demonising human beings or organisations," he said.

Vranitzky said his withdrawal from politics had nothing to do with his party's miserable performance in last October's European elections or that he had tired of an increasingly fractious relationship with his junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party.

"I thought that after so many years it would be a wise decision to transfer responsibility to younger people in the party," he said. "I've always maintained that 10 years should be considered as the utmost measure for a political career."
